title: Green wins the DTM opener at Hockenheim from pole
dek: Jamie Green led from pole to win the first race of the new two-race format for Audi, 2.327 seconds clear of Pascal Wehrlein, in a race with two safety cars and eight retirements.

chapters.title: A new weekend format and a deep field
text: The 2015 DTM season opened at Hockenheim on 2 May with a weekend built differently from recent seasons: two races instead of one, each with its own 20-minute qualifying session. Saturday brought a 40-minute sprint with no compulsory stop, Sunday a race of about an hour in which a tyre change was required. The calendar behind it ran to nine weekends and 18 races, taking in the Lausitzring, the Norisring, Zandvoort, the Red Bull Ring, Moscow, Oschersleben and the Nürburgring before a second visit to Hockenheim.

Marco Wittmann arrived as champion, carrying the number 1 on his BMW Team RMG M4, but the field he had to beat was deep. Audi, BMW and Mercedes-AMG each fielded eight cars, and former champions such as Mattias Ekström, Mike Rockenfeller and Gary Paffett were among the 24 starters. Lucas Auer, in the #22 Euronics/BWT Mercedes-AMG, and Tom Blomqvist, in the #31 BMW Team RBM, were making their DTM debuts.

The new schedule was already a talking point before the first start. With two races inside 24 hours, team bosses worried about their parts budgets, and after the first race BMW’s motorsport director pointed to the short gaps between sessions and the small repair windows after each race.

chapters.title: Green takes pole by 0.116 seconds in a very tight field
text: Jamie Green set the pace early and nobody could answer. His 1m33.044s in the #53 Audi Sport Team Rosberg car earned pole by 0.116s from Pascal Wehrlein, whose gooix/Original-Teile Mercedes-AMG managed 1m33.160s. Edoardo Mortara’s Audi Sport Team Abt car took third on the grid with 1m33.331s, and the whole 24-car field was covered by only 1.124s.

Behind Mortara it was closer still. Nico Müller’s Rosberg Audi (1m33.338s), Paul di Resta’s Mercedes (1m33.340s) and Rockenfeller’s Phoenix Audi (1m33.342s) were all inside 0.011s of the Abt car, and Rockenfeller’s time was matched exactly by Adrien Tambay’s #27 Audi, which had to settle for seventh. Blomqvist was the best of the newcomers in eighth, ahead of Miguel Molina and Ekström.

The two biggest stories were at the back. Augusto Farfus had briefly lifted BMW to third with a late lap of 1m33.310s before his car stopped on track, and he was then sent to the back of the grid because he had too little fuel for the post-session check. Paffett joined him on the last row after his team broke parc fermé rules following the session. With both gone, Blomqvist was BMW’s best-placed starter; the champion Wittmann lined up 14th, Bruno Spengler 17th, Martin Tomczyk 18th and Timo Glock 20th.

chapters.title: Green gets away while the midfield fights
text: Green made the best start of the front runners and led into the first corners, building a gap while the pack behind him got tangled. Robert Wickens’ Silberpfeil Energy Mercedes was the first casualty and Timo Scheider’s Phoenix Audi followed, both out after the opening lap. Scheider said the steering wheel was knocked from his hand and that he had hurt his wrist, though a break was ruled out.

Blomqvist, whose BMW had been damaged in a lap-one collision, and Molina were also gone, after six and nine laps. At the front, the order behind Green changed on lap 4, when di Resta moved his Silberpfeil Energy Mercedes past Wehrlein for second.

chapters.title: Two neutralisations and a hairpin crash
text: Around half distance Daniel Juncadella put his Petronas Mercedes into the gravel at the Sachs curve and the safety car came out. The restart was quickly followed by more trouble among the Audis: Ekström and Tambay, in the #5 and #27 cars, tangled in a fight for position, leaving Ekström with a puncture that sent him to the pits and Tambay in the gravel. Ekström recovered only to 12th and Tambay to 15th.

One lap later Tomczyk lost control of his BMW braking for the hairpin and hit Paffett’s Mercedes, with Auer unable to avoid the wreckage. All three were out, and Paffett called it a “stupid, stupid move”. The second safety car followed, and Green controlled both restarts to keep the lead.

chapters.title: Wehrlein takes second back; Audi dominates the top six
text: Once the track was clear, little changed at the front. Green was never threatened and took the flag for his first win in an Audi, the ninth DTM victory of his career, after a lights-to-flag drive. The fight for the podium was the only live contest: di Resta, who also set the fastest lap, a 1m34.751s on lap 4, was running second until Wehrlein, whose tyres had lasted better, got back past on lap 23 of 26 and finished 2.327s behind the winner. Di Resta was third at 3.221s.

Mortara was fourth, 3.930s back, ahead of Rockenfeller and Müller, so four Audis finished in the top six against two Mercedes. The BMWs filled the remaining points places, led by Maxime Martin in seventh, with Glock a strong eighth from 20th on the grid, Wittmann ninth and Farfus tenth after starting 23rd.

Green said he had been quick at Hockenheim the year before without the luck, and that now everything had worked for him. His win put him top of the standings on 25 points, ahead of Wehrlein on 18, di Resta on 15, Mortara on 12 and Rockenfeller on 10.

facts.v: Juncadella’s stop at the Sachs curve and Tomczyk’s crash into Paffett and Auer each brought out the safety car, and Green won both restarts.
Green’s 1m33.044s was 0.116s quicker than Wehrlein’s 1m33.160s, in a field covered by 1.124s.

facts.v: Di Resta passed Wehrlein for second on lap 4, and Wehrlein took the place back on lap 23 of 26.
Timo Glock’s BMW Team MTEK car started 20th and finished eighth, a gain of twelve places.
